candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Idealism need not imply conscious control over reality, but Bradley's appeal to an unstructured felt real risks conflicting with the unavoidable categorization built into perception.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn uses the host's first-person pragmatist framing and ends by directly asking how Bradley handles perceptual categorization.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move distinguishes perspective-dependence from voluntary mental control while pressing whether Bradley's account can accommodate cognitively structured perception.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The preceding idealist account that truth remains wholly within experience and that feeling encounters reality directly.

candidates.contextSummary: After Hawkins argues that thought and feeling never escape experience, Folley grants ordinary mind-framing but questions whether any accessible experience is genuinely prior to categorization.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradleyan truth resembles operational coherence plus further constraints from felt reality and intellectual satisfaction, so idealism does not make truth whatever one chooses to think.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly answers Folley's question, interprets Bradley and Russell, and presents the position as a pragmatism-plus conception.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This response supplies a constraint on idealist truth that answers the charge of arbitrary coherence and connects thought to action, feeling, and practical failure.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's concern that mind-framed truth may look mentally controllable or reducible to an arbitrarily coherent system.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins invokes operational coherence to explain why a merely consistent imagined world is not actual: attempts to act on false claims encounter failure and force revision.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Reflective agents cannot consciously recover wholly unstructured experience, yet precognitive feeling remains the foundation of thought and is ultimately integrated with structure in the absolute.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same answering speaker explicitly takes up the second question, repeatedly names Bradley, and develops the idealist account through the absolute.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers the perceptual-categorization objection while explaining how Bradley avoids identifying ultimate reality with either raw feeling alone or discursive structure alone.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's objection that perception appears categorically structured from the outset and offers no accessible stage of unchopped experience.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins concedes that metacognitive reflection always structures experience, treats raw feeling as an inaccessible foundation, and locates completed truth in a union of feeling, thought, and volition.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Bradley's absolute requires clarification because it may be either a Peircean regulative ideal for inquiry or an independently real endpoint whose existence Bradley confidently affirms.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn compares Bradley with C. S. Peirce in the host's pragmatist vocabulary and concludes with an explicit question about Bradley's certainty.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The question isolates whether the absolute performs only a methodological role or adds a substantive metaphysical commitment beyond pragmatic inquiry.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's claim that complete truth culminates in the absolute where thought, feeling, goodness, and beauty finally unite.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley compares Bradley's endpoint with Peirce's indefinitely approached perfect theory and asks whether the absolute must actually exist rather than merely guide inquiry.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradley is not agnostic about the absolute: complete truth must exceed thought, and the normative drive toward truth already recognizes the greater reality of its fulfillment.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker calls the preceding question excellent, explicitly answers that Bradley is not agnostic, and supplies Bradley-specific reasons.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response defends the substantive reality of the idealist endpoint by grounding it in the normativity and intelligibility of inquiry rather than treating it as a convenient fiction.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's comparison of the absolute with Peirce's possibly unreal regulative ideal and his question about Bradley's certainty.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins argues that a settled theory cannot itself be complete reality, but inquiry's orientation toward fulfillment treats that completion as more real than present partial understanding.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: The absolute may be understood more modestly as the amplified practical presupposition that intellectual, moral, and aesthetic progress are possible.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn offers a down-to-earth analogy involving researchers and asks whether Bradley's absolute is an expanded version of their practical faith.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move proposes a pragmatist reconstruction of the absolute that preserves its action-guiding role while testing whether stronger metaphysical claims are necessary.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's argument that normative striving recognizes the absolute as a genuinely real completion rather than a mere fiction.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley compares faith in the absolute with researchers' disposition to assume that a solution is possible, extending the analogy across intellectual, aesthetic, and moral progress.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Inquiry presupposes an intelligible attainable end, and idealism makes this intelligibility less accidental by joining knower and known rather than positing an inaccessible independent reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker affirms Folley's analogy and then develops Bradley's idealist explanation, consistently referring to Bradley in an expository voice.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move argues that idealism explains the possibility and direction of inquiry better than a naturalistic picture containing realities that may be wholly disconnected from experience.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Folley's proposal that the absolute is simply the practical faith presupposed whenever people pursue intellectual, moral, or aesthetic progress.

candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins accepts the presuppositional analogy but argues that Bradley treats the goal as real because it directs inquiry and because reality cannot be separated from experiential relations.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Philosophical theories are shaped by the questions and aims they serve, so reductive claims that one theory exhausts reality illegitimately exclude aspects they cannot explain.
candidates.attributionBasis: The guest answers a closing personal question, cites Ockham's razor and Collingwood, and restates the anti-reductive philosophical outlook developed earlier.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument directly resists naturalist reduction by tying theoretical adequacy to inquiry's purposes while preserving rigorous investigation of realities beyond any single framework.
candidates.contextSummary: Hawkins describes an insight about question-relative theorizing that led him away from desert-landscape reductionism toward rigorous but open-ended attempts to account for experience as a whole.

candidates.speaker: Joe Folley
candidates.proposition: Anti-reductionism still requires defensible admission standards, because inquiry must avoid both scientistic exclusion and an unrestricted free-for-all.
candidates.attributionBasis: The host explicitly responds to the tension in Hawkins's answer, states his distance from scientism, and identifies the pragmatic maxim as his current approach.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the compatibilist-pragmatist pressure on expansive idealism: openness to phenomena must be paired with standards that constrain what inquiry accepts.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Hawkins's rejection of reductive theories and his call to pursue comprehensive philosophy without dismissing what a theory cannot explain.

candidates.contextSummary: Folley agrees that scientism can be too restrictive but retains its demand for standards, presenting the selection of non-reductive yet non-permissive criteria as the central difficulty.

candidates.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
candidates.proposition: Bradley and William James share substantial pragmatist ground, but Bradley treats experienced urges toward truth and morality as evidence of an ultimate reality that genuinely draws inquiry onward.
